item.title: Don’t forget why learning is important
item.description:
This is a timed post. Every 5 minutes while writing this post, I had to stop to do 13 push-ups, and when I could no longer complete my required number, I had to upload it. My friends thought this would be a fun challenge, but it means that it will likely be less polished than some of my other output.


Summary:

Many people moving into AI safety are told that to succeed, they should read a lot and “try to develop takes.” However, it’s important not to forget why knowledge is important: it helps you do better things in the real world. 

Epistemic status: Pretty confident in the main claim (you should focus on learning the most valuable things), but less confident in the specifics of what things are the most valuable. I apologize if my language is too strong at times. 


“I dunno; it seems good to know things?”

The world is filled with ambitious young people, some of whom care about AI risks. Throughout my summer, I’ve gotten to talk to many of them. They visit San Francisco and Berkeley to talk to all the cool AI safety workers, or they go on surprise trips to work on high-impact, time-limited opportunities. Throughout this process, many of them look for jobs, and if they can’t find them, they seek out advice on how to get good enough to land one. 

A common piece of advice for how to get a job in AI safety is “read a lot and try to develop good takes.” This advice is featured very broadly, even for people who never intend to take a technical research role:

  • Matt Beard: "You don't have to be confident, but you should have something to say. It's fine to keep your views loosely held and defer to experts well, but you should take ownership over forming your own takes. Hiring managers will also want to hear your thoughts and reasoning."
  • 80,000 Hours: 
    • “A rough rule of thumb is to aim to read three or so AI papers a week to get a sense of what’s happening in the field, the terminology people use, and to be able to discriminate between real and fake AI news.”
    • “(No matter how you plan to do AI safety advocacy), it will be important for you to build up your AI safety knowledge.”
  • Kairos: “Succeeding in (generalist) roles requires real mission alignment and enough context to spot high-EV opportunities that someone without that background would miss.

As this knowledge propagates, I worry that many people who hear this advice lose track of why it’s important. Many people sharing this advice don’t spend a lot of time explaining why it’s valuable for everyone in AI safety to have their own takes. 

It’s obvious why you would want to know things if you’re trying to become a knowledge expert: knowledge experts are people who know things. However, if you’re trying to become a competent chief of staff, event manager, or field builder, or you want to take one of the many other neglected generalist or org scaling roles, it’s not as obvious why you should read everything. It’s good to have an explanation for why what you’re doing is impactful, but when I ask newcomers why they think it’s important to read, I often get answers like, “I dunno, it seems good to know things?” 

I worry about this. When people don’t have a good picture of why they’re doing something, they might overestimate something’s impact and miss its end goal. If you want to do good things, this is important to avoid.


Knowledge is only as valuable as what it allows you to do.

Knowledge is valuable because it helps you make better decisions. Orgs want people to be knowledgeable because people who know specific things about AI safety can do impactful things, not because storing more facts about AI is intrinsically valuable. You should focus on gaining the knowledge and tools that help you make better decisions. 

To do this, I recommend using a process I call directed reading: identifying the most important questions that will help you make better decisions and doing everything you can to get answers to those. This doesn’t necessarily have to be reading: it can be listening to a podcast, talking to a friend, or chatting with an LLM. But the primary goal is to resolve your most important uncertainties.

Here are some examples of uncertainties you may have:

  • If you’re still not sure if AI safety is the most important thing to work on, you can ask yourself, “What is the most important problem in the world to work on?” I don’t think people ask themselves this question enough.
  • If you’re new to AI safety and interested in learning all the important “context” that employers keep asking for, you can ask yourself, “Why is context valuable, and how can I most quickly answer the set of important questions that having context answers?”
  • If you want to start some impactful projects to build your skills, you can ask yourself, “What projects give me the most valuable skills, and what are the biggest needs in AI safety right now?” 
  • If you want to figure out what the biggest needs in AI safety are, you can ask yourself, “What does winning in AI safety look like, and what do we still need to do to make it to the finish line? In other words, what’s my theory of victory?”
  • If you hear that we need more generalists in AI safety, and you’re interested in solving this problem, you can ask yourself, “What problems are causing people to believe that we need more generalists, and how can I best address those specific problems?”[1]
  • If you plan to pursue any project, you can ask yourself, “Is this project really on the critical path to making AI go well? Do I have a coherent theory of change? Am I addressing a real problem?”
  • If you don’t want to get forever bogged down by infinite questions, you can ask yourself, “When is it safe to defer?”

To answer many of your questions, you’ll probably need to find answers to smaller and more fundamental questions. On its surface, your process might seem to replicate the original “read a lot of things” advice. However, by focusing on what you’re actually hoping to achieve with your knowledge search, you can develop critical skills much faster than you would by passively consuming the next 80,000 Hours podcast episode.[2] 

You can also double-check your learning processes. If the knowledge you’re getting doesn’t help you make better decisions, you should be willing to quickly pivot to trying other things. Learning things does not intrinsically save lives. Misalignment risk isn’t reduced by the number of books you’ve read from cover to cover. Don’t waste time memorizing social passwords and storing fake knowledge.[3] Do what will help you do good things in the real world.


Other things to keep in mind

While focused learning is important, I don’t think directed reading is the best way to solve all of your problems. 

First, while directed reading can be one of the best ways to resolve your largest uncertainties, you don’t need to spend all of your time skimming posts to find only the answers you need. Reading things you enjoy is pretty awesome, and you shouldn’t force yourself to spend all your time engaging with material that feels like homework. Find ways to integrate your study time into your routine, but don’t forget to do the things that make you happy. 

Second, pure information consumption might not be the best way to gain skills and understanding. Writing can be a valuable tool to help you internalize and understand various ideas, as well as keep track of any uncertainties you might still have.[4] Additionally, if nobody’s written about the thing you want to say, you should consider polishing your notes and publishing them online. If it helps, you can assemble a group of friends and do a timed writing challenge to publish the scraps you have lying around. 

Finally, you might be completely wrong about what you think you should be studying, or you might be missing some valuable new leads by continuously taking a focused approach to learning. To address this, it can be valuable to introduce some randomness into your media diet: find some time to read things (especially highly recommended things) that you don’t expect to be helpful. However, I suspect that most people aren’t spending enough time trying to learn things directly.

In the immortal words of the great Thomas Henry Huxley (aka “Darwin’s Bulldog”), “The great end of life is not knowledge, but action.”

  • By the end of the first draft, I had done 390 push-ups.
  • At publishing, I had done 468 push-ups.

item.title: What Mormons get right about community building
item.description:
Mormons get a lot of things right. Apart from strange Masonic temple rituals, they lead rather normal—and even excellent—lives. Mormons enjoy a longer lifespan,[1] Utah is the #1 state for volunteering,[2] and their language training programs are so successful that missionaries are a known source for foreign service and intelligence careers.

Throughout this post, I'll be making generalizations of Mormons rather than hedging the claims properly. I grew up in Wisconsin, Maryland, and Utah, and many of the claims are more true of the Utah/Idaho/Arizona corridor (affectionately called the "Morridor" by some ex-Mormons) than the rest of the US, and certainly the rest of the world.

Religions share much in common with AI safety and other impact-driven movements, and even more so the Mormon church. There are a few reasons for this:

Commitment to the cause. Anecdotally, nearly all of the ~500 Utah Mormons I've interacted with have been true believers, and only a handful just went to church out of habit.[3]

High stakes. Mormons do believe (I've heard they are trying to disavow this, but it was taught) that they will get a planet or some portion of the cosmos as their own if they are good in this life, and become Gods of their own. This is not far off from many transhumanist utopic visions. However, it's also true that they believe that before God's Second Coming, the world will go into a state of war and disarray, not unlike the forecasts of extinction-level risks bearing fruit.

Urgency to attract new members. Given the stakes, it's not a hard followup to believe that you should do what you can to teach more people about the awesome[4] benefits and risks awaiting them. Talent-constrained movements feel a similar urgency that is a little more impact-focused than community-focused.

Insularness. It's hard to be friends with someone outside the church, since being a member is a significant social and time commitment, and most people (in Utah) you interact with are members anyway. This contributes to both a sense of community and lack of viewpoint diversity.

Building community is a first-order priority

Mormons' focus on fostering community enables them to be effective at all the non-religious stuff they do.

Geography

First, some background: wards are composed of perhaps 50 to 100 families. There's no shopping around for congregations—ward membership is determined by where you live. This facilitates getting to know people. Each Sunday, the whole ward gets together for services, which are sometimes followed up by potlucks. Wednesdays, the kids get together for activities. Saturdays are for a rotating schedule of cleaning the church. Throughout the week, families are often close enough together that they see each other frequently.

Ministering

Within a ward, families are assigned a pair of people that minister to them: visit them once a month to check in, and maybe go over a spiritual lesson. While in the worst case these feel contrived, oftentimes people feel like they can count on their ministers to support them. With a few rotations of these over the years, you begin to develop a network of people that you wouldn't have naturally become friends with. This parallels the adage of "you get most job opportunities from acquaintances, not close friends": creating connections from across the network helps everyone to be fewer degrees away from each other.

Trek

Every four summers, the youth of the ward recreate the Mormon pioneers' crossing of the plains. In true 1800s fashion, they pull handcarts. A particularly exciting phase of this when I went involved the "Womens' Pull", where only the girls pulled and pushed the handcarts. (I think this was to simulate the number of men who died during the crossing). Afterwards we learned how to square dance. The only inauthentic aspect was how delicious the food was; we weren't served gruel. As my grandmother has often stated, "They didn't have McDonald's back then", and this increased our shared gratitude. Most of all, it increased our friendship.

Callings

Adult ward members are assigned callings, which range from choir director to primary instructor (children's religion classes) to bishop (equivalent of a pastor or imam). Callings aren't application-based, and a former bishop might be called to run nursery, the Sunday activities for toddlers. This flattens the hierarchical structures that would otherwise arise. Additionally, switching positions over the years helps each ward member feel connected to others, no matter their skills or interests that would normally push them to certain roles in the workforce.

Fast offerings

On the first Sunday of every month, Mormons hold a 24-hour fast from eating and drinking, aside from the sacramental rituals of eating a gob of (normally white) bread and a thimbleful of water. Aside from making the Sunday dinner delicious, Mormons save fast offerings, payments meant to cover the expenses of what they would have paid on food. Young men go door to door, collecting these payments (this is increasingly not the case; when I was doing it at 14, many people paid online. But they did give me amazing frozen Hershey's almond bars, which they made us promise not to eat until after breaking our fasts). The offerings go to the Bishop's Storehouse, where the money is converted into food for the hungry. The only other thing I heard about that place was that they had the best chocolate milk.

Being ingroupy allows you to move faster

When there is a shared value framework, people develop trust quicker. Upon moving into a new ward, a Mormon family will immediately have a community of like-minded people who do similar activities to them. Since they don't have to figure out whether they have to watch their tongues while discussing their morals, they can put more energy into getting to work and learning more about the people around them.

This also enables Mormons to dedicate more time resolving the surface-level issues, rather than revisiting foundational differences when interacting with others.

Do I think it's worth it to increase the ingroupy-ness of mission-driven movements? Not necessarily. Viewpoint diversity matters a lot more when the answers aren't legislated. Ingroupy-ness also limits the number of people who can join the movement.

Implications

Here are a few ideas vaguely inspired by Mormonism:

  1. Create a platform for facilitating virtual 1-1s, especially between people from distinct backgrounds or positions
  2. Create a travel grants program, so that people can benefit from geographic proximity
  3. Instead of e.g. donating 10% of your income, precommit to donating a 24-hour period of your time each month to helping other people

Overall, I think we could do well by taking cues from other movements that have succeeded—in one way or another—at building community.
